column3: Affirms that the sky-and-earth order is purposeful, supporting the meaningfulness of the former owners' removal.
Directly contrasts the focus: the challenged opponents are told to act without any granted delay.
The granted reprieve to Iblis supplies the clear contrary condition to the former owners' denial of reprieve.
Explicitly states that, once the decisive angelic event arrives, people will not be reprieved.
Immediately begins the inventory of the gardens and springs the destroyed people left behind.
Cosmic administration across sky and earth provides only broad temporal context for the withheld respite.
Links rejection to seizure after blessings from sky and earth, closely paralleling the estate's loss.
Names God as the giver of both laughter and weeping, directly framing the focus's denied mourning.
A second explicit grant of limited reprieve to Iblis sharpens the contrast with 44:29.
Their inability to rise or defend themselves parallels a destruction from which no extension follows.
Continues the immediate catalogue of the cultivated estate and honorable station abandoned by them.
Divine ownership of sky and earth and universal return offers only general cosmic framing.
Sky and earth can become instruments of sudden collapse, qualifying the security of those beneath them.
The transformed sky supplies a cosmic contrast to the sky that does not weep in the focus.
The kingdom of sky and earth is broad background, not a clarification of mourning or respite.
Punishment sent from the sky after wrongdoing supports the focus's pattern of decisive consequence.
Immediately identifies the ease and enjoyment in which the former owners had lived.
Its rebuke for laughing instead of weeping forms a direct emotional contrast to the focus's no-mourning image.
The commanded reversal from brief laughter to much weeping directly connects tears with deserved recompense.
Provision from sky and earth is only distant background to the estate and its dispossession.
The command to inspect the camel does not clarify cosmic mourning or the denial of respite.
The failed exchange of guidance for error does not add a focused link to the ayah.
Immediately completes the transfer: the abandoned estate is inherited by another people.
Divine dominion and return offer a general frame but do not develop the focus's two claims.
Its creation and comprehensive knowledge formula is only broad sky-and-earth context.
The sky opening into gates provides a transformed-cosmos contrast to its non-mourning in 44:29.
Reflection on human origin does not clarify mourning, destruction, or respite.
It joins reflection on sky and earth with the possibility that the appointed term has drawn near.
Idris's elevation has no focused connection to the ayah's loss or withheld delay.
The constructed sky is a remote cosmic counterpart without a mourning or judgment relation.
It directs observers to the end of stronger earlier peoples, a close historical lens for Pharaoh's people.
Water descending from the sky to flourishing gardens contrasts with the former owners' now-abandoned estate.
Weeping in humbled response to revelation supplies a clear contrary instance of meaningful tears.
The isolated act of looking adds no relevant account of mourning or reprieve.
The chosen prophets' prostration and tears provide a positive contrast to the focus's absence of cosmic grief.
The Lordship of sky and earth supplies broad setting for the named cosmic witnesses.
The question about disbelief does not itself clarify the focus's mechanisms.
The watchful ambush of Hell supports the certainty of an awaiting consequence, not an extension.
Helpless witnesses looking on at death parallel the irreversible moment behind the denied respite.
The brothers' performed tears contrast with the focus's declaration that neither sky nor earth mourned.
The sky's melting at the final event gives a cosmic transformation contrast to its withheld weeping.
The blessed looking from couches does not illuminate the focus's emotional or temporal claim.
It pairs grave wrongdoing with humiliation and harsher final punishment, supporting irreversible consequence.
Feeding during famine does not clarify the focus ayah.
Waiting for angels or the divine command ends in consequence for people who wronged themselves, without further delay.
Mutual waiting anticipates a decisive outcome, but it does not itself state the refusal of reprieve.
The demand to know when the promise will arrive connects expectation with an approaching decisive event.
No one can escape in earth or sky or find another protector, reinforcing the focus's total abandonment.
The comprehensive record of hidden things does not clarify mourning or respite.
The fate of earlier deniers provides a general precedent for the rejection of Pharaoh's people.
All that is in sky and earth glorifies God, creating a contrast with the focus's explicitly absent cosmic mourning.
The oath by the Lord of sky and earth confirms truth generally without developing the focus.
Mutual counsel to patience and mercy has no focused relation to the ayah.
Divine encompassing possession of sky and earth is broad background only.
The purposeful creation of sky and earth and warning to deniers support a meaningful, not arbitrary, downfall.
The appointed Day of Decision directly clarifies why a final outcome does not admit renewed respite.
Their later question, "Will we be reprieved?", directly voices the futile request negated in 44:29.
The nearby assertion that sky and earth were not created for play reinforces the purposeful judgment around 44:29.
The removal of mountains belongs to irreversible final transformation, a secondary contrast to the focus's aftermath.
At the near punishment people inspect their own deeds and wish to be dust, showing an irreversible reckoning.
Passing by sky-and-earth signs while turning away supplies a broader explanation for failed response before consequence.
The absence of concern even between intimate friends parallels the focus's picture of complete abandonment.
Iblis explicitly asks for delay until resurrection, the requested possibility denied to the people in 44:29.
It names Pharaoh with Qarun and Haman, their arrogance, and their inability to outrun the consequence.
The command for beautiful patience does not clarify mourning or the former owners' lost respite.
Measured creation and dominion are general framing rather than a direct link to the focus.
Unjust rejoicing on earth is assigned a punitive consequence, closely qualifying the former owners' enjoyment.
Explicitly states that on the Day of Decision disbelievers will not be reprieved.
The spreading of the earth does not clarify the ayah's mourning or temporal claim.
Divine possession of sky and earth remains a general cosmic formula here.
Sky and earth stand by divine command and the dead emerge at a call, framing the sovereignty behind final outcomes.
Explicitly combines unrelieved punishment with the statement that they will not be reprieved.
Divine knowledge of speech in sky and earth is not a focused clarification of the focus ayah.
The question of who created sky and earth exposes the deniers' lack of certainty behind their false security.
It commands travel and observation of the criminals' end, making past destruction an interpretive evidence source.
A punishment dispatched from the sky gives a secondary sky-to-judgment relation.
It directs observers to examine the outcome of deniers, closely paralleling the retrospective force of 44:29.
A creditor's humane postponement is a legal and positive contrast to the denied reprieve after judgment.
Signs in sky and earth do not benefit a people unwilling to believe, giving a broader precondition for ruin.
The paired command to wait shows a fixed approaching outcome rather than equal control over time or reprieve.
It calls for observing earlier peoples' end and explicitly states that God destroyed them.
Sky, earth, and mountains respond to the Trust with awe, contrasting with their absence of mourning for the former owners.
It directs travel to inspect the end of earlier associationists, a close historical parallel to Pharaoh's fate.
The keys of sky and earth establish divine control generally but do not develop the focus's result.
Divine knowledge and the written record are general background, not a focused link.
The instruction on ambiguous speech does not clarify the ayah.
Its signs and life-giving rain offer broad sky-and-earth context, but not the focus's mourning or delay.
Exclusive dominion and the lack of any protector reinforce the former owners' total lack of support.
Misleading companions and the fulfilled word over prior nations support a settled, inherited pattern of loss.
It ties waiting to the destructive days of earlier communities, directly framing delay as an approaching historical consequence.
The earth's prepared expanse does not clarify the focus ayah.
The breadth of the earth for believers' worship does not illuminate the judgment scene.
Universal submission and return provide only a general cosmic counterpart to the focus's judgment.
If the requested angel descended, the matter would be decided and they would not be reprieved.
It identifies a sign amid repeated unbelief, a limited backdrop for the consequences in the focus.
The challenge ends with "do not reprieve me," directly using the focus's key term in a contrary setting.
The proportioning of the soul does not clarify the focus's claims.
The guilty wish to be leveled with the earth when concealment fails, a secondary image of final shame.
The denial of punishment supplies the false confidence overturned by the focus's completed judgment.
Reviving the dead earth is a distant contrast to the un-mourned removal of the former possessors.
Directly recalls the sea's division, Israel's rescue, and Pharaoh's people drowning, supplying the historical event behind the focus's aftermath.
Explicitly states that the condemned will neither have punishment lightened nor be reprieved.
Defines granted delay to disbelievers as an increase in sin, a crucial contrast to the focus's final refusal of delay.
Every community has a fixed term that cannot be advanced or postponed, directly clarifying the denied reprieve.
It names Pharaoh's people, their rejection of signs, and their drowning, directly supplying the cause and event presupposed by 44:29.
Gradual leading from where people do not know provides a temporal contrast to the completed, unextended judgment.
God's granting of respite before a firm plan is a direct counterpoint to the focus's statement that no respite remained.
The appointed term cannot be hastened or delayed, directly qualifying the finality of the focus.
Pharaoh's drowning and his belated declaration of belief directly precede the irreversible outcome recalled in 44:29.
The rebuke of Pharaoh's belief only after prior rebellion shows repentance arriving after the decisive threshold.
Pharaoh's body is preserved as a sign for later people, directly extending the aftermath of his destruction.
All in the heavens and earth prostrate, forming a meaningful cosmic-response contrast to their absence of mourning for Pharaoh's people.
Wrongdoers ask for a short delay when punishment is seen, directly echoing the lost possibility of respite.
No community can precede or postpone its term, directly stating the temporal boundary behind the focus.
Created things and their shadows prostrate to God, giving the cosmos an active response unlike the withheld mourning.
All creatures in the heavens and on earth bow to God, a cosmic-obedience contrast to the focus's no-mourning formula.
God postpones people until an appointed term, but when it comes they cannot delay it, directly clarifying no reprieve.
The seven heavens, earth, and all within them glorify God, the clearest positive cosmic-response contrast to their not weeping here.
Moses identifies Pharaoh's signs as a proof of his impending ruin, directly framing the focus's judgment.
Pharaoh seeks to expel Moses' people and is then drowned with all who were with him, directly supplying the event's conclusion.
The heavens nearly rupture, the earth splits, and mountains collapse at a grave false claim, showing that cosmic fields can react to moral violation.
Pharaoh pursues through the sea and is overwhelmed by it, directly narrating the destruction whose aftermath the focus states.
A town destroyed by divine judgment is barred from returning, strongly supporting the irreversibility of the focus's outcome.
Heavens, earth, sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, and creatures prostrate, extending the cosmic-response contrast.
No community can outstrip or delay its appointed term, directly reinforcing the no-reprieve claim.
At death the wrongdoer asks to return, directly presenting the futile request that follows a closed temporal threshold.
The requested return is denied by a barrier until resurrection, making the finality of lost opportunity explicit.
All in the heavens and earth, including birds, know their prayer and glorification, contrasting with the focus's withheld cosmic grief.
God saves Moses and those with him, providing the rescue side of the Pharaoh narrative immediately relevant to the focus.
The others are drowned, directly naming the destruction after which no mourning or reprieve is reported.
Pharaoh and his forces are seized and cast into the sea, directly describing the event behind 44:29.
God defers people until an appointed term, but when it arrives no delay is possible, directly matching the focus's temporal claim.
Moses is saved while Pharaoh's people are encompassed by the evil punishment, directly extending the same narrative judgment.
The sky and earth answer God's command willingly, another explicit image of cosmic responsiveness.
Pharaoh's people provoke divine wrath and are drowned, directly identifying the cause and execution of their downfall.
Their destruction makes them a precedent and example for later people, directly develops the focus's retrospective significance.
The immediately preceding section identifies Pharaoh's people as a tested people, establishing the narrative subject of 44:29.
Moses is commanded to take the servants by night because they will be pursued, directly setting up the final destruction.
The sea is left parted as Pharaoh's troops proceed to their drowning, an immediate narrative prerequisite for the focus.
The following verse contrasts the former owners with the Children of Israel, who are rescued from humiliating punishment.
It identifies Pharaoh as arrogant and transgressive, directly explaining the judgment just described.
Israel's choosing upon knowledge extends the contrast between the rescued community and Pharaoh's dispossessed people.
The signs given to Israel as a manifest trial continue the immediate judgment-and-rescue context.
Pharaoh is seized with his troops and cast into the sea, directly summarizing the destructive event.
At approaching death a person asks for a brief delay to act rightly, directly articulating the request foreclosed in 44:29.
God will not delay a soul when its appointed term arrives, directly restating the no-reprieve principle.
God grants the deniers respite while His plan is firm, a direct contrast to the focus's completed withdrawal of respite.
God may defer punishment to an appointed term, but that term cannot be delayed when it arrives.
The deniers are granted only a little respite, a limited-delay contrast to the focus's none.
The disbelievers are granted a brief respite, directly contrasting a temporary interval with the focus's final closure.
The earth reports its news on the final day, showing an active terrestrial witness where 44:29 denies terrestrial mourning.
The earth's report follows divine inspiration, strengthening the cosmic-witness contrast.
Those who followed false leaders wish for a return after the bonds between them are cut, a secondary post-judgment contrast.
God appoints a term and a specified term with Him, providing direct temporal background for the denied reprieve.
Those facing the Fire wish they could be returned, a secondary expression of the closed opportunity after judgment.
The oppressed people inherit the blessed land while what Pharaoh and his people built and raised is destroyed, directly paralleling the estate transfer in 44:25-28.
When the final interpretation arrives, the deniers ask whether they can be returned, a secondary return-after-closure parallel.
The Day is only deferred to a numbered term, directly supporting the focus's fixed temporal boundary.
Every term has a prescribed decree, supplying a general but direct framework for the end of respite.
Moses is commanded to travel by night with the servants and strike a dry path through the sea, directly preparing the Pharaoh judgment scene.
The sea parts for Moses into great mountain-like divisions, directly supplying the route that leads to Pharaoh's destruction.
The other party is brought near the parted sea, immediately preparing its drowning in the following verse.
The guilty ask to be sent back after seeing and hearing the truth, another secondary image of futile post-judgment return.
Destroyed generations do not return to those after them, supporting the irreversible departure implied by the focus.
The wrongdoer wishes for another turn in order to do good, a secondary expression of lost opportunity.
The condemned acknowledge repeated death and life and ask whether there is any way out, a secondary finality parallel.
Moses is sent with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, directly beginning the same narrative cycle concluded in 44:29.
The signs shown to Pharaoh's people establish the warning context before their final drowning.
Successive signs are shown so that Pharaoh's people might return, clarifying the prior opportunity before final closure.
Pharaoh's people ask Moses to remove punishment and promise guidance, showing a temporary response before their later destruction.
Pharaoh asserts dominion over Egypt and its rivers, a direct contrast to his later loss of control and estate.
Pharaoh's boastful disparagement of Moses supplies the arrogance behind the ensuing wrath and drowning.
The demand for visible ornaments or angels shows Pharaoh's people's resistant terms before the decisive outcome.
Pharaoh leads his people into heedless obedience, directly preparing their collective punishment.
Moses's mission to Pharaoh is explicitly named as a sign, placing Pharaoh's fate within an enduring warning pattern.
Pharaoh turns away in his power and calls Moses a sorcerer or madman, directly identifying the rejection preceding his seizure.
